planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring in bright, indirect light in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; Calandiva is grown as a flowering houseplant or patio pot, since it has no meaningful cold tolerance.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light or a few hours of gentle morning sun in well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried out. Calandiva is a compact florist kalanchoe bred for fully double, rose-like blooms held in dense clusters above glossy, scalloped succulent leaves, flowering far longer and more heavily than single-flowered kalanchoe types. Like other blossfeldiana selections it is a short-day bloomer, so it naturally flowers in winter and needs long, uninterrupted nights of darkness to reinitiate buds if you want to force a repeat bloom cycle. Remove spent flower clusters to tidy the plant and avoid soggy soil, which quickly rots the fleshy roots and stems.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Root stem or leaf cuttings in spring or summer in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; crinkle-leaf plant is grown as a container and houseplant succulent, since it is not reliably hardy outdoors.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light with a little morning sun in shallow pots of well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has fully dried. Crinkle-leaf plant produces low, clustering rosettes of thick, wavy-margined gray-green leaves tipped in reddish-bronze, with a distinctive fringe of pale aerial roots along the corky stems that helps it capture humidity from fog and dew in its native South African habitat. Its slow, clumping growth suits small pots, dish gardens, and windowsills, and offsets are easily separated once they develop their own roots. Leaf or stem cuttings root readily if allowed to callus for a few days before being set on dry succulent mix.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Root leaf or stem cuttings in spring or summer in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; Plover Eggs plant is grown as a small container and houseplant succulent.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light in shallow pots of well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried out completely. Plover Eggs plant forms clumps of plump, speckled, egg-shaped leaves mottled in purplish-brown flecks over gray-green, a pattern and shape that closely resemble the speckled eggs of a plover and give the plant its common name. It stays small and slow-growing, making it well suited to shallow succulent dish gardens and compact windowsill collections, and mature clumps send up thin flower stalks with small tubular pink-and-white blooms in summer. Propagate easily from individual leaves pressed lightly onto dry succulent mix, and keep water off the foliage to avoid spotting or rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in spring or summer in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; jade necklace is grown as a trailing container and houseplant succulent.

directions: Grow in bright light, including some direct sun, in well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried out. Jade necklace produces stiff, upright-then-trailing stems densely stacked with small, thick, rounded leaves that overlap in tight columns resembling a beaded chain or a stack of tiny green coins, an architectural form well suited to hanging baskets and raised pots where the stems can cascade. Cooler temperatures and bright light bring out a red blush along the leaf margins, intensifying the plant's color contrast. Stems are brittle and prone to snapping, so site the plant where it won't be brushed against, and trim and root fallen segments to fill out the container.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Root offsets or leaf cuttings in spring in well-drained, gritty succulent mix; Buddha's Temple is grown as a slow-growing collector's container succulent.

directions: Grow in bright light with some protection from the most intense midday sun in well-drained, gritty succulent mix, watering only once the soil has dried out. Buddha's Temple is a hybrid crassula prized for its tightly stacked, four-sided towers of thick, pale gray-green leaves that rise in a precise, architectural column resembling a miniature pagoda or temple. Growth is very slow and columns rarely branch on their own, so established plants are often propagated by removing and rooting basal offsets rather than relying on seed-grown stock. Keep the tightly packed leaf axils dry when watering to prevent rot from moisture trapped between the leaves, and provide excellent drainage year-round.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
